description: One original parallel-plate total-field diagram: right +|q| plate, left -|q| plate, six positive and six negative marks, two short outward leads and exactly six leftward gap-field arrows, with only the original E vector label. The n83 other-plate E/2 contribution remains in the prose; no E/2, force, distance, energy formula, extra charge or answer overlay is invented.

authoritativeText.text:
Energy in a charged capacitor
Electric charge is a property of matter associated with electric pushes and pulls.
Its signs are called positive and negative.

A conductor allows charge to move readily;
an insulator resists this flow and keeps separate conductors electrically separated.

A capacitor has conducting surfaces, called plates, separated by insulating material.

It stores separated charge and energy in the electric field between its plates.
An electric field describes the electric push or pull on charge at each place.
Energy can be transferred to produce changes, such as motion or warming.

Discharging, allowing the separated charge to flow through a suitable circuit, reveals this energy transfer.
Figure 158 shows a Leyden jar, an early capacitor.
Its inner and outer metal coatings are its two conducting surfaces, and the glass between them is the insulator.

A dedicated discharge tool can produce a spark between a small ball and a plate.
This describes a possible discharge, not a visible spark in the apparatus drawing or an instruction to touch a charged capacitor.

Released energy can become mechanical energy of motion, light, and heat.
For comparable discharge devices under similar conditions, a larger capacitance or a higher charging voltage usually allows more energy to be released and often a stronger spark.

For a fixed linear capacitor with equal opposite plate charges, capacitance is the charge amount on a single plate divided by the voltage size.
It is not the net charge of the two plates together.
Voltage, or potential difference, measures energy transferred per amount of charge moved between the plates.

We now derive the stored energy of a parallel-plate capacitor.
This is an ideal thought experiment, not a handling instruction.
Parallel plates are flat surfaces facing each other at a constant separation.

Use an ideal model with plates so broad that edge effects, changes in the field near their edges, can be ignored.
Between them is vacuum or a homogeneous, linear dielectric with negligible energy loss.

Vacuum is space without material;
a dielectric is an insulator whose bound charges can shift slightly in an electric field.
Homogeneous means its relevant properties are the same throughout, and linear means its response scales with the applied field.

In the model, let the facing plates carry equal amounts of opposite charge, with no added external field.
Disconnect the power supply first, keeping each plate's charge fixed.
Slowly change the plate separation without changing the plate area or material properties.

If the total field strength between the plates is $E$, the contribution of a single plate acting on the other is $\frac{E}{2}$, as discussed in §81.
The section mark refers to a numbered section of the book.

The equal charge amounts give equally strong contributions.
Between the plates these point in the same direction, from the positive plate toward the negative one, so they add.

Each contribution is therefore half the total.
Here E means field size, and the fraction means half that size.

In Figure 159, the charge $q$ spread over a plate's surface feels the other plate's uniform field, a field with the same strength and direction throughout the region.
Do not also count the plate's own field as a force pushing that same plate.

In Figure 159, the left plate's sign is negative and the right plate's sign is positive.
The bars on charge labels give the charge amount without its sign.

The leftward arrows show the total field direction from the positive plate to the negative plate, not charge-flow paths.
The accent above E indicates direction as well as size.

Plain E in the calculation is the field size.
The picture shows the total field, while the force calculation uses only the other plate's half-field contribution.

Work is energy transferred by a force as something moves.
Using the electric potential-energy formula (8-22) for a charge in a uniform field, calculate the work as one plate is held still and the other slowly approaches it.

The charged plates attract, and the attraction is the plate-charge amount multiplied by the other plate's half-field.
At fixed charge, unchanged area, and the maintained ideal material conditions, this force stays constant.

Work for a constant force in the direction of motion is force multiplied by distance.
The complete relative distance is the initial gap d, not an arbitrary shorter movement.

The stored field energy tends to zero as that gap tends to zero in the ideal model.
This zero-gap limit is our zero-energy reference, so the full positive work done by the field equals the initial stored energy.

This gives $E_P=|q|\frac{E}{2}\cdot d$.
Here $|q|$ is the charge amount on a single plate without its sign, and $d$ is the plate separation.

E with the lower P labels the stored energy.
The equality sign means both sides describe the same quantity, and the adjoining factors and centered dot mean multiplication.

This expression already counts the energy of the plates' interaction;
do not count that same interaction again for the other plate.

In this uniform-field model, $Ed=|V|$ is the size of the voltage between the plates.
The bars mean the amount without its positive or negative sign.

Field size multiplied by separation gives this voltage size.
The capacitor's energy can therefore be written as charge amount multiplied by voltage size, divided by two:

With the plate charges fixed in this ideal process, slowly bring the plates closer as the separation approaches zero.
The work done by the electric field equals the initial stored energy.

Reversing that same fixed-charge relative movement separates the plates against their attraction.
It requires the same work from outside and restores their stored field energy.

This mechanical reverse movement is distinct from electrical charging, which changes the plate charge.
Reversible electrical charging with negligible loss also converts the work supplied from outside into stored energy.
Reversible means that the ideal process can be undone without a lasting energy loss.

If the plates remain connected to a supply, moving them also allows charge and energy to be exchanged with that supply.
Mechanical work then cannot simply be equated to the change in the capacitor's stored energy.

Direct charging from a fixed-voltage supply can also dissipate energy in the circuit, transferring it into heat and other forms.
Do not count all energy supplied as stored capacitor energy.

Use the capacitance relation (8-36) to replace either the voltage or the charge amount in equation (8-42).
This gives equivalent ways to express the same stored energy.

C denotes capacitance;
a fraction bar means divide what is above it by what is below it.
A squared quantity means that quantity multiplied by itself:
The earlier formula uses U for voltage, whereas this lesson uses V for the same potential-difference quantity.

Capacitance is plate-charge amount divided by voltage size, so voltage size is charge amount divided by capacitance.
Replacing voltage this way gives the charge amount multiplied by itself, divided by capacitance and then by two.

Equivalently, charge amount is capacitance multiplied by voltage size.
That replacement gives capacitance multiplied by voltage size and by that same voltage size again, divided by two.
These are ways to calculate the same energy, not separate energies to add together.

These formulas are not limited to parallel-plate capacitors.
They also apply when the capacitor's shape is fixed and its dielectric is linear with negligible energy loss, so its capacitance does not change with charging voltage.
Do not extend this statement to nonlinear devices whose capacitance changes with voltage, or ignore losses such as leakage, charge escaping through imperfect insulation.

A thundercloud and an area of ground below it can be roughly modeled as a very large capacitor.
This model describes lightning as a discharge, whose flash and thunder reveal a powerful release of energy.

Real lightning is complex.
This simplified model helps explain stored energy and discharge;
it is not a complete way to calculate the energy of every lightning event.

Using Soviet electricity prices of its own time, the original book valued such a discharge at "no more than a few kopeks," small units of money.
This is a historical rough estimate, not a universal lightning energy or a present-day electricity bill.

The book's $10^{-6}$ seconds means a millionth of a second.
It is a local rapid-discharge time scale used in that simplified description, not the total duration of every lightning event.
Concentrating energy in a short time and a small space produces strong local effects, helping explain lightning damage.

Applications of capacitors
The common small capacitors discussed in the original book usually stored less than a few hundred joules.

A joule is a unit of energy.
This describes devices of that time, not a universal upper limit on capacitor energy.

Real capacitors gradually lose energy through leakage.
How long they retain it depends on the device and operating conditions.

Different devices can retain their energy for different lengths of time.
For the long-term power-supply purposes discussed in the book, those capacitors cannot generally replace rechargeable batteries.

Capacitors can nevertheless act as short-term energy sources.
Specially designed large-capacitance devices and capacitor banks, connected groups, can also store energy.
Do not apply the limitations of the book's device examples to every capacitor.

Capacitors have practical uses as energy-storage devices.
They can accumulate energy and release it through a suitable circuit in a time much shorter than the charging time.

The book's "almost instantaneous" means such a rapid pulse discharge, a brief burst, not that every capacitor empties immediately in any circuit.
Both the capacitance and the circuit determine how quickly discharge happens.
This controllable rapid release is widely useful.

For example, a camera flash can first use a battery to charge a capacitor.
The capacitor's discharge current, the flow of charge, then makes the flash lamp light up.
Storing energy and releasing it quickly supplies the bright light needed for a photograph.

The original book lists radio technology as a major capacitor application and continues that topic in grade ten.
This is its course arrangement, not a claim that capacitors serve only radio technology.
They also store energy and serve other roles in many kinds of circuit.

inventory.description: Two separated, upright parallel plate strokes in one frame; the left plate is negative and the right positive. Both have the same projected length.
One short horizontal lead protrudes outward from the left plate and one from the right plate, at approximately the same middle height. They are unconnected outside the diagram.
Six minus marks are arranged vertically just inside the left plate.
Six plus marks are arranged vertically just inside the right plate, corresponding to the negative rows.
The outer upper labels are -|q| beside the left plate and +|q| beside the right plate. These are signed plate charges, not extra point charges.

Six straight, approximately equally spaced horizontal field arrows span the same gap, all pointing LEFT, from the positive right plate to the negative left plate. They are perpendicular to both plates.
An E with the conventional vector accent is above the upper field line. It denotes the total gap field, not an E/2 label or a force arrow.
